The Midnight Market: A Memory Returned
Thorne sold the night they met. Caelan bought it back. Nobody asked Thorne.
At a fae market where memories are the currency, Caelan buys back the night he fell in love — and learns it's the night Thorne was locked in.

Once a year the Midnight Market opens at the crossroads, and anything you remember can be sold into a lantern. Caelan finds Thorne's lantern on a shelf — their first meeting, still glowing — and buys it back, only to learn Thorne sold it on purpose. While Kai trades away a failure, Ronan refuses to choose for him, and Silas keeps the ledger honest, you decide from Caelan's side whether to return a memory, hold it, or let a man forget the night you can't.
A market guide who knows every stall, every price, and the one rule: what you sell is gone from your head, not from the ledger.
If Caelan decides for him, Thorne gets the night back — and loses the right to choose it.

The Lantern Stall
Ask why he sold it — before anything else
The lantern stall
Midsummer night, 11:40 PM
The Midnight Market opens once a year, at the crossroads, for one night. At the lantern stall, every lantern holds something somebody used to remember.
I have just paid for one. Inside, small as a dollhouse: a garden gate, white moonflowers, and me, seven years younger, holding them through the bars.
Thorne, in the market guard's grey, lifts the lantern off the counter before the merchant can wrap it. He reads the tag. It's in his own handwriting.
Someone sold our first meeting.
I bought it back.
You should have asked why I sold it.
I open the ledger to last Midsummer. Entry 212. Seller: Thorne. Item: one night, garden gate. I don't read the reason aloud. It isn't mine to read.
A year. He's been missing that night for a whole year, and I've been telling it to him over dinner like a bedtime story.
What does Caelan do first?
Ask him why. Then just listen.
Why did you sell it? I'm not asking so I can argue. I'm asking so I know.
I don't remember the night. I remember the reason, because I wrote it on the receipt so I'd believe myself later: ‘So I stop hearing the lock.’
That's all I have. Everything else is in that lantern. Including you.
Caelan asked why before anything else; Thorne said he no longer remembers the night, only the reason on his receipt: so he'd stop hearing the lock.
Promise to keep it shut until he's ready.
I won't open it. I won't even keep it on me. Tell me when you want to talk, and I'll wait.
I hand the lantern to Silas instead of to him. It's not a punishment. Silas has the only neutral pair of hands in this market.
Held, not sold. Entry 212, annotated. Nobody opens it without Thorne present.
Caelan promised not to open the lantern; Thorne gave it to Silas to hold, and no one may open it without Thorne present.
Tell him it's your night too.
It's my night too, Thorne. I was there. You don't get to sell half of something we both have.
I set the lantern down very carefully, like it might go off. Then I step back from it, and from him.
You were there for the flowers. You weren't there for the rest. That's the half I sold.
Caelan claimed the night as his too; Thorne set the lantern down, stepped back, and said Caelan was only there for the flowers.
The Bridge
Let one night be two different memories
The footbridge over the market canal
Midsummer night, 12:15 AM
The footbridge over the market canal is strung with paper charms. Below, sold memories drift past in bottles, faintly lit, going wherever bought things go.
I cut through the Night Garden on a dare. There was a guard at the gate, so I gave him moonflowers through the bars. We talked until I had to run home.
That was the night they bound me to that gate and locked me in it. I know because I wrote it down before I sold it. I don't remember it.
Every time a lock turns at night, my hand still shakes. The market takes what happened. It doesn't take what it did to you.
You remember the flowers. I remember the lock.
I open my mouth to defend the flowers. Then I close it. Both things happened. I was just on the free side of the bars.
I thought he was guarding the gate. He was the one locked behind it. For seven years I've called that romance.
A bottle bumps the bridge pillar below and spins on. Neither of them watches it go.
What does Caelan say about that night?
Say it out loud: both versions are true.
Both happened. The flowers and the lock. I won't make you trade one for the other to keep me comfortable.
I lean on the rail next to him. Not touching. Close enough that I would, if I wanted to.
Across the canal, a shout. Kai stands at the buying stall with his hand flat on the counter, and Ronan is very carefully not stopping him.
Thorne. Caelan. Kai's about to sell something, and he asked for witnesses who won't talk him out of it.
Caelan said out loud that both the flowers and the lock were true; Thorne stood beside him at the rail, close but not touching.
Ask for a minute with it. Don't argue.
I need a minute with this. Not to argue. To stop picturing the flowers without the bars.
Take it. I've had a year.
Across the canal, a shout. Kai stands at the buying stall with his hand flat on the counter, and Ronan is very carefully not stopping him.
Both of you. Kai's selling something tonight, and he asked for witnesses who won't talk him out of it.
Caelan asked for time to absorb Thorne's side without arguing; Thorne gave it.
Defend the flowers. They were real.
The flowers were real, Thorne. I won't pretend that night was only a cage.
Nobody asked you to. I asked you not to make it only a garden.
Across the canal, a shout. Kai stands at the buying stall with his hand flat on the counter, and Ronan is very carefully not stopping him.
Argue later. Kai's selling something tonight, and he asked for witnesses who won't talk him out of it.
Caelan defended the flowers as real; Thorne said he only asked Caelan not to make the night only a garden.
The Buying Stall
Each person sells, keeps, or holds — and nobody chooses for anyone
The buying stall
Midsummer night, 12:40 AM
The buying stall is a cart hung with empty lanterns. Kai's hand is flat on the counter. Ronan stands one step behind him, on purpose.
The Silver Road. The guy with the shortcut map, the handshake, the whole stupid week. I want it gone.
Without it, you'll believe the same promise again.
We can carry it with you. We can't choose it for you.
I look at Ronan for a long time. He doesn't nod. He doesn't shake his head. So I decide. I sell it.
Dust-colored light fills a lantern: a road, a handshake, a folded map. Kai blinks like a man who walked into a room and forgot why.
Recorded. Kai no longer knows that week. Ronan and I still do. That's the price of having witnesses.
Every eye drifts to the other lantern on the counter: a garden gate, white flowers, and a lock nobody can see from outside.
I could open it right now. I've wanted to for an hour. Thorne is watching my hands.
What does Caelan do with Thorne's lantern?
Hand it to Thorne. He decides what returns.
I pick it up by the base, not the latch, and hold it out. My hand only shakes a little.
I take it. I don't open it. I give it to Silas to hold until I know which part I want back, if any.
Held for Thorne. Entry 212. The choice is his, and so is the timing.
Caelan handed the lantern to Thorne unopened; Thorne left it in Silas's keeping until he decides which part, if any, to restore.
Keep it sealed. Be willing to start over.
Keep it sealed. If he never wants it back, I'll introduce myself like a stranger and hope I'm good at it.
You'd do that? Meet me like we never met?
I'd rather meet you twice than make you remember once against your will.
I tie a holding cord around the lantern. Sealed. Not restored, not sold. Entry 212, held.
Caelan chose to keep the lantern sealed in Silas's holding and said he'd rather meet Thorne again as a stranger than force the memory.
Open it for him. He'll thank you later.
I unlatch it. Just a crack. Light spills out — not flowers. A bolt sliding home, iron on iron, loud as a gunshot.
I'm on my knees before I know why. Ten seconds of the lock, back in my head, and nothing else. Not the flowers. Not the dawn.
I snap the shutter closed and take the lantern. ‘Restoring without the seller's hand is theft twice. Ten seconds got out. The rest stays shut. Recorded.’
You gave me back the worst ten seconds of it.
Caelan opened the lantern without consent; Thorne involuntarily regained ten seconds of the lock and nothing else, and Silas confiscated the lantern and recorded it.
The Blank After
Let what's sold stay gone; record new facts as new
Silas's ledger tent
Midsummer night, 1:30 AM
Ledgers stack to the canvas ceiling. Silas folds away an old caravan map. Kai stops him and points to a symbol in the margin: a silver line, crossed out twice.
Why did I draw this?
That belongs to what you exchanged.
Do you want an explanation?
Not the memory. Just the warning.
Recorded as new: ‘Cheated on the Silver Road by a man selling shortcuts. Chose to forget how. Don't buy shortcuts.’ You'll know it like a rumor, not a scar.
And ask before we fill any other blank.
I turn to Caelan. ‘You're a witness to Thorne's night. I can take down your account too — as new information, for him, only if he ever asks.’
My version. The flowers without the bars. He's heard it for a year, at dinner, nodding. I don't know anymore if that was kind.
What does Caelan do with his account of that night?
Ask Thorne, right now, if he wants it.
Thorne. Silas can write down what I remember of that night. Do you want it to exist at all? You can say no.
Write it down. Don't read it to me. And put the bars in it.
I record it as a sealed witness account, readable only by Thorne. Caelan adds the bars himself, in the second line.
Kai's warning was recorded as new information; Caelan asked Thorne first, and at Thorne's request his account was sealed for Thorne alone, bars included.
Write it, seal it, and tell him it exists.
I dictate it plain. Flowers, bars, the moment I ran home. Silas seals it before I can soften anything.
He'll be told it exists. Not what's in it. I don't keep secret copies for anyone, including people I like.
Fine. It exists. I'll decide later if it's mine.
Kai's warning was recorded as new information; Caelan's account was written and sealed, and Thorne was told it exists but not what it says.
Decline. He's heard your version enough.
No. He's heard my version every week for a year. I think that's part of why he sold it.
I look at him for a long second. Then I nod, once. It's the first thing tonight he's gotten exactly right.
No account recorded. Kai's warning stands alone on the page.
Kai's warning was recorded as new information; Caelan declined to record his own account of Thorne's night, and Thorne approved.
Closing Bell
Give Thorne the choice — at your own cost
The market square, stalls folding
Midsummer night, 3:10 AM
The closing bell rings every hour now. Stalls fold like paper. The Lanternwright announces that held lanterns go back on sale at dawn unless someone pays to redeem them.
The price for Entry 212 is a memory of equal weight. The market likes victories. They burn bright.
I know exactly which one. The Winter Tourney. The final bout, the crowd, the second I knew I'd won. My best day that isn't about him.
I can give you the key.
Not the answer.
I set the lantern on the cobblestones between us and step back. Two full steps. Far enough that I can't reach it first.
For the record, he's very proud of that tourney. He tells it constantly.
Then maybe it's time I stopped telling things constantly.
How does Caelan pay for the key?
Pay with the Winter Tourney. Give him the key.
The Lanternwright draws the Tourney out of Caelan like a thread from a hem: a crowd, a final bout, a roar. Then it's in a lantern, and not in him.
Kai. You're looking at me like I should know something. Did I win something once?
You did. You were insufferable about it. Now you're not. Fair trade.
I take the key. It's warm from his hand. He doesn't ask what I'll do with it. He just looks at the lantern, then at me, and waits.
Caelan sold his memory of winning the Winter Tourney to buy the key and gave it to Thorne; Caelan no longer remembers that he won.
Ask Thorne first. Split the price if he wants.
Before I pay — do you want me to? Or would you rather owe me nothing for this?
Half. Sell the final bout, keep the rest. I'll pay the other half with my first winter on this gate. Cold, boring, mine.
Two threads go into the Lanternwright's lantern. Caelan loses the last bout but not the win. Thorne loses one cold winter. The key goes to Thorne.
At Thorne's choice they split the price: Caelan sold the Tourney's final bout and Thorne sold his first winter as gate guard; Thorne holds the key.
Keep your victory. This one is his to pay.
I won't buy your night for you. If I pay, it's a little bit mine again. It has to be yours.
I pay with my first winter on this gate — cold, boring, mine. I don't need anybody's best day to get my own night back.
Redeemed by the seller. Caelan's Tourney stays where it is. Entry 212: key issued to Thorne.
Caelan declined to pay so the night would stay Thorne's; Thorne redeemed it with his first winter as gate guard and holds the key.
At the Gate
Update his memory exactly as he chooses — no more, no less
The market's west gate
Midsummer night, 4:20 AM
The west gate, an hour before dawn. Thorne kneels by the lantern with the key. The Lanternwright has shown him how: one turn per part. Flowers. Lock. Dawn.
Three parts of one night. I sold all three to lose the middle one. Turns out the middle one stayed in my hands anyway.
I want to remember that I got out.
Then that's where our next story starts.
One turn. Pale light climbs Thorne's arm: a latch giving way, wet grass, a road walked alone at sunrise, moonflowers crushed in a pocket.
I remember. The latch gave at four in the morning. I walked out. I walked for six hours. The flowers were still in my pocket when I stopped.
He got out alone. I'd already gone home. I never even knew there was that part.
Two parts still glow inside the lantern: the flowers, and the lock. The key is still in Thorne's hand.
What does Caelan ask for, if anything?
Nothing. The rest stays his to decide.
The rest is yours. Leave it in there for a year, or forever. I won't ask on anniversaries.
I lock the lantern with the key and hang it on my belt. Two parts inside. One part back where it belongs.
Restored: dawn. Held by Thorne: flowers, lock. Caelan knows only what he was there for. Recorded.
Thorne restored only the dawn he walked out in; Caelan asked for nothing, and Thorne keeps the flowers and lock sealed on his belt.
Ask once about the flowers. Accept any answer.
One question, then I'm done. Will you ever want the flowers back? ‘I don't know’ is an answer.
I don't know. Not tonight. Maybe not with you standing right there.
I nod and step back again. He hangs the lantern on his belt, sealed. Flowers and lock, together, undecided.
Thorne restored only the dawn; Caelan asked once whether he'd ever want the flowers back, accepted 'I don't know,' and Thorne kept the rest sealed.
Ask him to take the flowers too.
Take the flowers too. Please. That part has me in it. I need you to have it.
No. You need it. I don't. Stop asking me to want your version.
Thorne locks the lantern with two parts still inside and keeps the key. Caelan doesn't ask again. Not asking again costs him something visible.
Thorne restored only the dawn; Caelan pleaded for him to take the flowers too, Thorne refused, and the flowers and lock stayed sealed in his keeping.
A New Way Out
Build a new shared moment without reaching for the sold one
The back road out of the market
Midsummer night, 4:50 AM
Thorne doesn't take the old bridge. He turns left at the cider stall, down a narrow road nobody uses, toward the market's back gate.
This is not where we met.
I know this road. I chose it.
He knows it from the dawn he just got back. Six hours of walking out. A road I've never once seen.
May I walk with you?
To the gate.
And after?
Ask when we get there.
Behind them, Kai and Ronan argue gently over the map with the crossed-out silver line. Kai is the one holding it.
How does Caelan walk this road?
Walk beside him. Ask about after at the gate.
I walk on his left, half a step behind on the narrow parts. At the gate I ask, plainly: after?
Breakfast. Somewhere neither of us has a memory of. Then we'll have one.
I'd like that. I'd like that a lot.
Caelan walked Thorne's chosen road beside him and asked about after at the gate; Thorne invited him to breakfast somewhere new, and Caelan said yes.
Walk with him as a friend. Don't ask yet.
I walk him to the gate and don't ask about after. He notices. I can tell by how long he holds the latch.
You didn't ask.
You'll tell me when there's an after worth asking about. I'm good at waiting now. I've practiced all night.
Caelan walked Thorne to the gate as a friend and chose not to ask about after, leaving it to Thorne to bring up.
Let him walk it alone. Say goodbye here.
This road's yours. I'd only be visiting it. Go. I'd rather say goodbye properly than follow.
I take his hand for a second. Just one. Then I walk the road the way I walked it the first time — alone, and out.
Caelan stays at the cider stall until the lantern on Thorne's belt is too small to see.
Caelan let Thorne walk his road alone and said a proper goodbye; Thorne held his hand for a second and left.
The Lantern on the Ground
Choose a new beginning — or the distance to keep
Outside the back gate
Midsummer dawn, 5:30 AM
First light. The market folds itself into the hillside. Silas stands at the back gate with the ledger open to Entry 212, the last open line of the night.
Before I close the book: Thorne holds a lantern with two parts sealed inside. Whatever happens to them gets written down. That's the only promise I make.
I don't remember the Silver Road. I just know not to take it. Weirdly freeing.
You chose that. I didn't. That's the part I'll remember.
I set the lantern on the grass between me and Caelan. I want him to see it's there. I want to see what he does when it's in reach.
Seven years ago I handed him flowers through bars. Tonight he's handed me the bars, to see whether I'll open them.
The lantern glows faintly on the grass: a garden, a gate, a lock no one can see from outside. Nobody moves for a long moment.
What does Caelan do with the lantern on the ground?
Leave it. Ask him what you are now.
I don't touch the lantern. I look at him instead. ‘What are we now? Not seven years ago. Now.’
Someone who got out. And someone I'm choosing, on a road I picked. Ask me again tomorrow. The answer will be the same.
I write: Entry 212, held by seller, unopened by choice. New entry: one breakfast, not yet eaten. They both initial it.
Caelan left the lantern untouched and asked what they are now; Thorne chose him again as a partner on his own terms, and the lantern stays sealed by Thorne's choice.
Let the flowers go. Introduce yourself.
I nod at the lantern. ‘Let the flowers go, if you want them gone. I'll keep my copy. I'll never tell it again.’
Thorne turns the key once. The flowers lift out like pollen and are gone for good; only the lock stays, sealed. Silas records the release.
Hello. I'm Caelan. I'm visiting.
Thorne. I guard this gate. By choice.
Thorne released the flowers forever and kept the lock sealed; the romantic first meeting now exists only in Caelan's untold memory, and they introduced themselves anew.
Open it. All of it. He should know.
I pick up the lantern and open it all the way. Flowers and lock pour out together and go into him at once.
I remember everything. The flowers were lovely. The lock was louder. And you just did it again — decided for me.
I write it exactly: Entry 212, restored in full, without consent, by Caelan. The line stays. If there's ever a repair, it starts here.
You gave me the key once. Then you took the answer.
Caelan forced the full restoration; Thorne now remembers the whole night and left alone, and Silas recorded the non-consensual restore as the basis for any future repair.
A Road We Picked

Thorne keeps the dawn he walked out in, and the right to keep the rest sealed. Caelan stops telling the flowers story and starts asking questions instead; they agree, out loud, to be partners on a road neither of them has a memory of yet. Kai leaves with a warning instead of a wound, holding his own map.
I got out. This time I'm walking toward something.
Hello, I'm Visiting

Thorne lets the flowers go for good, and the romantic first meeting now lives only in Caelan's head, where it stays untold. They start over like near-strangers — names, a handshake, a breakfast that could be the first of something or of nothing. Ronan and Kai take the long road, on purpose.
Thorne. I guard this gate. By choice.
Restored in Full

Caelan opens the lantern and Thorne gets the whole night back — flowers, lock and all — and walks away with it, alone. Silas's ledger records exactly who decided what, and the line stays: if there is ever a repair, it starts from that entry, not from a blank.
You gave me the key once. Then you took the answer.
